questions.q: What does `parent: sqlServer` on the `sqlDatabase` resource actually do?
options: Declares the database as the server's child, so Bicep automatically knows the database can't be created before the server, without an explicit dependsOn
Deletes the parent server whenever the database is deleted
Has no functional effect — it's purely a comment
Forces the database to use the same name as the server
questions.explain: This is the same automatic-dependency mechanism from Lesson 12, applied to a real server-and-database pair.

questions.q: Why is `sqlAdminPassword` declared with `@secure()` instead of a plain `string` type with a default?
options: @secure() tells Bicep never to log or output the value anywhere, and it must be supplied at deploy time rather than hardcoded
@secure() makes the parameter deploy faster
@secure() is required for every string parameter in Bicep, regardless of sensitivity
There is no real difference between @secure() and a plain string parameter
questions.explain: A plain string parameter with a default risks the password being visible in deployment history, logs, or the file itself — @secure() prevents that.

questions.q: What's actually different about deploying Azure SQL compared to deploying a Storage Account (Lesson 8), per this lesson?
options: The shape — Azure SQL is a server-and-database pair (parent and child), while a Storage Account was a single resource on its own
Azure SQL cannot be deployed with Bicep at all
Azure SQL requires a completely different CLI tool
There is no meaningful difference between the two
questions.explain: The mechanics — resource block, name, deploy command — are identical; only the resource shape (single vs. parent-child pair) differs.

questions.q: Why check the Azure Portal's deployment history after a deployment, if the CLI already reported success?
options: It's a second, independent confirmation that the deployment actually succeeded and shows every resource it touched
The CLI's success message cannot be trusted under any circumstances
The Portal is the only way to run a Bicep deployment at all
Checking the Portal is purely optional and provides no additional information
questions.explain: Confirming success from two independent places — the CLI's exit code and the Portal's own record — is good practice, not redundant.

questions.q: According to this lesson, where should a secret like a SQL admin password actually come from at deploy time?
options: A Key Vault reference, an environment variable, or a CI/CD secret — never hardcoded in the file
A plain-text default value written directly into the .bicep file
It should be typed manually into the Azure Portal after every deployment
Secrets are not needed for Azure SQL deployments
questions.explain: Lesson 20 covers CI/CD secrets specifically — this is the same principle of keeping secrets out of the file itself.
